title: Cache Workbench
lede: A cache is a small, fast shelf of copies in front of a big, slow store.
blurb: A cache is a small, fast shelf of copies in front of a big, slow store.

exps.title: Shorter freshness
exps.change: TTL 60 s → 6 s · a card now leaves the rack ten times sooner
exps.question: What happens to the share of requests answered from the rack?

exps.title: A smaller rack
exps.change: Rack 12 slots → 4 slots · a third of the room
exps.question: The rack can now hold 4 of the 40 records. The hit rate…

exps.title: No favourites
exps.change: Popular traffic → even traffic · every record equally likely
exps.question: Same rack, same TTL, but no record is more popular than another. The hit rate…

exps.title: The rack is emptied
exps.change: Empty the rack while traffic flows · a deploy, a restart, a flush
exps.question: Right after the rack is emptied, how long do requests take?

exps.title: A record changes
exps.change: Record #1 is updated in the archive · its card is still in the rack
exps.question: Of the next reads of #1 answered from the rack, how many show the old version?

title: Pub/Sub Workbench
lede: Publish/subscribe lets one part of a system announce something without knowing who listens.
blurb: Publish/subscribe lets one part of a system announce something without knowing who listens.

exps.title: More subscribers
exps.change: Subscribers 2 → 5 · three more stations now want every message
exps.question: The press now feeds five stations instead of two. How long does it spend on each message?

exps.title: A slow subscriber
exps.change: Station C takes 2 s per card · the press still prints one every 1.2 s
exps.question: After two minutes, what has happened?

exps.title: A subscriber goes away
exps.change: Station C is offline for 20 s · its subscription is not durable
exps.question: The cards printed while C was away…

exps.title: Crash before the ack
exps.change: Stations crash 1 time in 10 after doing the work, before stamping the card
exps.question: Over 100 messages, how many times does station A's handler run?

exps.title: One queue, two workers
exps.change: A and B read from one shared queue instead of each having a subscription
exps.question: Of 100 messages, how many does each of A and B get?

blurb: A load balancer decides which server gets each request, and that one decision sets how long users wait.
title: Load Balancer Workbench
lede: A load balancer decides which server gets each request. That one decision, made thousands of times a second, sets how long users wait.

exps.title: One more counter
exps.change: Counters 3 → 4 at 0.9 parcels/s · a third more capacity, same traffic
exps.question: What happens to the slowest 5% of waits (p95)?

exps.title: One slow counter
exps.change: Counter 1 works at a third of the speed · 4 counters, round robin
exps.question: With round robin, what happens to p95?

exps.title: Uneven parcels
exps.change: 1 parcel in 10 takes 11× longer than the rest · same total work
exps.question: Switching from round robin to least connections changes p95 by…

exps.title: A counter crashes
exps.change: Counter 2 dies · the balancer only finds out at its next health check
exps.question: With a health check every 30 s, how many parcels fail?

exps.title: Sticky customers
exps.change: Two customers send 40% of the parcels · sticky sessions pin each customer to one counter
exps.question: Twenty customers in total. What happens to the counters?

title: Circuit Breaker Workbench
lede: When a service you depend on gets slow or fails, the danger is not the failed calls: it is your own workers waiting on them.
blurb: When a service you depend on gets slow or fails, the danger is not the failed calls: it is your own workers waiting on them.

exps.title: The supplier slows down
exps.change: Supplier healthy → slow · each call now takes about 6 s · no timeout, no breaker
exps.question: Three in ten requests never call the supplier. What happens to them?

exps.title: Add a timeout
exps.change: Slow supplier, as before · timeout off → 1.5 s
exps.question: With a 1.5 s timeout, what happens to the requests that need the supplier?

exps.title: Add the breaker
exps.change: Supplier failing · timeout 1.5 s · breaker off → on (opens after 5 failures in a row, 5 s cooldown)
exps.question: With the breaker on, what happens to the load on the supplier?

exps.title: Retry three times
exps.change: Supplier failing, fixed after 20 s · timeout 1.5 s · retries 0 → 3, no backoff, no breaker
exps.question: The cause is fixed after 20 s. With three immediate retries per request, when do supplier calls succeed again?

exps.title: A long cooldown
exps.change: Supplier failing, fixed after 20 s · timeout 1.5 s · breaker on · cooldown 5 s → 30 s
exps.question: With a 30 s cooldown, how soon after the fix does traffic flow again?

title: Rate Limiter Workbench
lede: A rate limiter hands out permission at a fixed pace and says "not now" (HTTP 429) when it runs out.
blurb: A rate limiter hands out permission at a fixed pace and says "not now" (HTTP 429) when it runs out.

exps.title: A bigger bucket
exps.change: Bucket 8 tokens → 16 tokens · refill stays at 4 per second
exps.question: Clients want more than the limit all the time. How many requests get through per minute now?

exps.title: The window boundary
exps.change: Fixed window (8 per 2 s) vs token bucket (4/s, holds 8) · a client sends 16 just before a window ends and 16 just after
exps.question: With the fixed window, how many get through in that 0.4 s?

exps.title: One noisy client
exps.change: Client C sends 8 requests/s, A and B send 1/s · one shared limit of 6/s vs a third of it per client
exps.question: With one shared limit, what happens to A and B?

exps.title: Retrying on 429
exps.change: Client A bursts 30 requests at once · impatient clients retry every 0.25 s vs clients that wait the Retry-After time (plus jitter)
exps.question: How many rejected attempts does the limiter see?

exps.title: Two app instances
exps.change: 1 → 2 app instances behind a load balancer · each keeps its own bucket in memory (4/s, holds 8)
exps.question: Clients ask for 7.5 requests/s. How many get through per minute now?

blurb: Retries feel safe, but when many clients retry at once they keep a system overloaded long after the fault is gone.
title: Retry Storm Workbench
lede: A retry feels like the safe thing to do: if a call fails, try again. When many clients do it at once, retries can keep a system overloaded long after the original problem is gone.

exps.title: Three quick retries
exps.change: No retries → 3 retries, sent at once · then a rush of 16 visitors
exps.question: Without retries, the trouble from a rush is over in about ten seconds. With three immediate retries, how long does it last?

exps.title: Wait before retrying
exps.change: Immediate retries → exponential backoff · wait 2, then 4, then 8 s
exps.question: Clients now wait on the benches before trying again. What happens after the rush?

exps.title: Add jitter
exps.change: Exponential backoff → backoff with jitter · each wait spread between ½ and 1½ times its delay
exps.question: The average wait is exactly the same as before. What does jitter change?

exps.title: A timeout that's too short
exps.change: Timeout 3 s → 0.8 s · the window normally takes 0.7 to 1.3 s · no rush
exps.question: Nothing else is wrong. With three retries, what share of the window's work reaches a client who is still waiting?

exps.title: Retries at every layer
exps.change: 1 layer retries → 3 layers retry (app, client library, proxy) · 3 retries each
exps.question: In the worst case, how many attempts reach the window for one request?

title: Hash Ring Workbench
lede: When data is split across nodes, every key needs a home, and adding or losing a node should move as few keys as possible.
blurb: When data is split across nodes, every key needs a home, and adding or losing a node should move as few keys as possible.

exps.title: Add a node, modulo style
exps.change: bin = hash mod n · nodes 4 → 5
exps.question: One node joins a cluster of four. What share of the 1,000 keys has to move to a different node?

exps.title: Add a node, on a ring
exps.change: Hash ring, 1 marker per node · nodes 4 → 5
exps.question: Same change, but keys go to the next marker clockwise. Which keys move?

exps.title: Is the ring fair?
exps.change: Hash ring, 5 nodes · 1 marker per node
exps.question: Five nodes, one marker each, placed by hashing. How much does the busiest node get compared with a fair fifth?

exps.title: A node fails
exps.change: Hash ring, 5 nodes, 1 marker per node · node C fails
exps.question: C's keys must go somewhere. Where do they go?

exps.title: One very popular key
exps.change: Hash ring, 100 markers per node · key 7 gets 30% of all requests
exps.question: Does consistent hashing spread a hot key's traffic?

title: Canary Deploy Workbench
lede: A canary deploy sends a small share of real traffic to the new version, watches it, and either rolls it back or promotes it.
blurb: A canary deploy sends a small share of real traffic to the new version, watches it, and either rolls it back or promotes it.

exps.title: How many people does a bad build hurt?
exps.change: Bad build (1 in 5 orders fail) · canary 25% → 1% · automatic rollback on
exps.question: At 25%, the rollback arm catches the bad build after about 11 failed orders. At 1%, how many orders fail before it is caught?

exps.title: A rare bug
exps.change: 1 order in 200 fails on the new build · canary 10% → 1%
exps.question: At 10% the arm needs about 2 hours to be sure. At 1%, how long?

exps.title: A twitchy rollback
exps.change: Good build at 10% for 2 hours · threshold normal → tight (any failure above 0.15%)
exps.question: The new build is fine. Both tracks fail 1 order in 1,000 by bad luck. How often does the tight rule roll it back anyway?

exps.title: Who sees what
exps.change: Good build at 25% for 10 minutes · 100 users, each ordering about 7 times
exps.question: With random routing, how many users see both the old and the new version?

exps.title: The bug that doesn't fail
exps.change: New build charges the wrong price on 3 orders in 10 · canary 10% · promoted after a 30-minute bake
exps.question: The rollback arm only watches failures. After an hour, how many wrong-price orders went out?

blurb: Two full copies of production: deploy to the idle one, flip all traffic with one switch, keep the old one ready.
title: Blue-Green Workbench
lede: Run two complete copies of production. Deploy the new version to the idle one, then move all traffic over with one switch, and keep the old one ready to switch back.

exps.title: Roll back a bad release
exps.change: Green ships with a bug that fails 40% of requests · the alarm fires 15 s after the flip
exps.question: You roll back by flipping the gate back to blue. How long until errors stop, compared with redeploying the old version server by server (one minute each)?

exps.title: What it costs
exps.change: A normal deploy · blue is kept running after the flip so you can roll back
exps.question: What do you pay for that instant rollback while the deploy is in progress?

exps.title: A cold green
exps.change: Green starts with an empty cache · you flip as soon as it is up
exps.question: Right after the flip, what happens to latency?

exps.title: Flip without draining
exps.change: Draining off · blue stops the moment the gate flips
exps.question: What happens to the requests already on blue's lane, in its queue or under its presses?

exps.title: A migration blue can't read
exps.change: Green's migration drops a column blue still reads · then green turns out to be bad
exps.question: You flip back to blue. What happens?

title: Rolling Deploy Workbench
lede: A rolling deploy replaces a service one piece at a time, so it never has to stop.
blurb: A rolling deploy replaces a service one piece at a time, so it never has to stop.

exps.title: Take more bays out at once
exps.change: maxUnavailable 1 → 3 · busy traffic (2 requests/s, six bays serve 3/s)
exps.question: Half the bays may now be out at the same time. What happens?

exps.title: Add before you remove
exps.change: maxUnavailable 1, maxSurge 0 → maxUnavailable 0, maxSurge 1 · busy traffic
exps.question: Now a new bay is added before any old one is taken out. What does that cost?

exps.title: No readiness probe
exps.change: Readiness probe on → off · a new bay's flag rises as soon as it is installed
exps.question: The new version is fine, but every module needs 6 s to warm up. Without the probe…

exps.title: A broken version
exps.change: Next version: broken · it starts, but never passes its health check
exps.question: With the readiness probe on, how far does the rollout get?

exps.title: Two versions at once
exps.change: Next version saves user data in a new format that the old version cannot read
exps.question: During the rollout, old and new bays both serve. What do users see?

blurb: An index is a sorted copy of a few columns that points back to the rows: fast lookups, paid for on every write.
title: Index Workbench
lede: An index is a second, sorted copy of a few columns that points back to the rows. It turns read-everything into look-it-up, and every write pays to keep it current.

exps.title: The table grows ten times
exps.change: 10,000 → 100,000 rows · query ISBN = … · a catalogue on ISBN
exps.question: A full scan gets about 10× slower. How much slower does the lookup through the ISBN catalogue get?

exps.title: A third catalogue
exps.change: 100,000 rows · catalogues: ISBN → ISBN, author, author + year · adding books
exps.question: You add two more catalogues so more queries are fast. What happens to adding a new book?

exps.title: The wrong end of a composite
exps.change: 100,000 rows · one catalogue sorted by author, then year · query: year = 1969
exps.question: The catalogue holds year on every card. What does the librarian do for a year-only search?

exps.title: An index on a yes/no column
exps.change: 100,000 rows · a catalogue on 'on loan' · 4 in 10 books are on loan
exps.question: You ask for every book that is on loan. What does the planner choose?

exps.title: The title is on the card
exps.change: 100,000 rows · titles by one author · catalogue on author → catalogue on author that also carries the title
exps.question: How much does it help when the card already carries the title?

blurb: How a list API remembers where the last page ended decides how fast deep pages are and whether rows repeat or vanish.
title: Pagination Workbench
lede: Every list API has to hand data out a page at a time, and the way it remembers where the last page ended decides how fast deep pages are and whether rows get shown twice or never.

exps.title: A deep page
exps.change: 20,000 rows, 20 per page · page 1 vs page 500
exps.question: How much more work is page 500 than page 1?

exps.title: New rows while you page
exps.change: Offset paging, 10 pages of 20, newest first · about one new row per second while the reader pauses 2 s between pages
exps.question: What does the reader see?

exps.title: Rows deleted while you page
exps.change: Offset paging, 10 pages of 20 · about one row deleted per second from the rows being paged
exps.question: Now rows disappear from pages already read. What does the reader miss?

exps.title: A cursor on created_at alone
exps.change: Cursor paging, 10 pages of 20 · rows are imported three per second, so created_at has ties · cursor key created_at vs (created_at, id)
exps.question: With WHERE created_at < :last, what happens at page boundaries?

exps.title: Jump to page 37
exps.change: 20 per page · a user clicks page 37 directly
exps.question: How does each kind of pagination get there?

blurb: Concurrency is one worker juggling many tasks by switching between them. It hides waiting but adds no extra hands.
title: Concurrency Workbench
lede: Concurrency is one worker keeping many tasks in progress by switching between them. It hides waiting, but it never adds a second pair of hands.

exps.title: Dishes that mostly simmer
exps.change: 4 dishes, each 3 s of stirring and 70% simmering · one at a time → switch when a pan starts simmering
exps.question: How much sooner is everything served?

exps.title: Dishes that never simmer
exps.change: 4 dishes, each 3 s of nonstop stirring · one at a time → round robin, 1 s each
exps.question: Does taking turns help when there is no waiting at all?

exps.title: A very short turn
exps.change: Round robin, 4 nonstop dishes, switching costs 0.3 s · turns of 3 s → 0.3 s
exps.question: What share of the cook's time goes on moving between pans?

exps.title: One huge stew
exps.change: A 12 s stew and four 1 s dishes, all nonstop, stew first in line · finish each step before moving → round robin, 1 s turns
exps.question: What happens to the four small dishes?

exps.title: More pans on the stove
exps.change: Keep every pan busy, 70% simmering · 4 pans → 8 pans
exps.question: What happens to dishes served per minute, and to the time each dish takes?

blurb: Parallelism is many pieces of work at the same instant. More workers help only as far as the work can be split.
title: Parallelism Workbench
lede: Parallelism is doing many pieces of work at the same instant, on several cores or machines. More workers help only as far as the work can be split, shared things allow and coordination costs.

exps.title: Eight workers
exps.change: 1 → 8 workers on 8 benches · 10% of the job is packing, which only one station can do
exps.question: How much faster does a job finish?

exps.title: More workers than benches
exps.change: 8 → 16 workers · still 8 benches (cores) · job split into 16 chunks
exps.question: What happens to the job time?

exps.title: One shared tool
exps.change: Shared tool off → on · the last 40% of every chunk needs the one tool on the rack
exps.question: With 8 workers, how fast is the job compared with one worker?

exps.title: A tiny job
exps.change: A job of 0.3 s instead of 16 s · 1 worker with 1 chunk vs 8 workers with 8 chunks
exps.question: Which finishes first?

exps.title: One heavy chunk
exps.change: Uneven data: the first eighth of the job holds a third of the work · 8 chunks vs 32 chunks, 8 workers
exps.question: With 8 chunks, what happens to the job time?

blurb: Async I/O lets one worker start many slow operations and handle each result when it's ready, instead of waiting.
title: Async Workbench
lede: Async I/O lets one worker start many slow operations and handle each result when it is ready, instead of standing still while it waits.

exps.title: Four waiters or one
exps.change: 100 orders · each waits 200 ms in the kitchen · 4 blocking threads vs 1 async waiter
exps.question: Which finishes the 100 orders faster?

exps.title: Orders that need real work
exps.change: 100 orders · 40 ms of CPU each, 10 ms in the kitchen · 4 blocking threads vs 1 async waiter
exps.question: Now most of the time is spent working, not waiting. Which is faster?

exps.title: Await in a loop
exps.change: 20 orders · async · `for … await` one by one vs `Promise.all` / `asyncio.gather`
exps.question: How much faster is gathering them?

exps.title: Gather a thousand
exps.change: 1,000 orders · gather all at once vs at most 20 in flight · the kitchen has 32 burners, calls time out after 2 s
exps.question: Which way gets more orders delivered?

exps.title: One blocking call
exps.change: 100 orders · async · each handler also reads a file synchronously for 15 ms
exps.question: What happens to the batch?

blurb: JavaScript runs your code on one thread, one task at a time. Timers, network replies and drawing all wait their turn.
title: Event Loop Workbench
lede: JavaScript runs your code on one thread, one task at a time. Everything else, from timers to network replies to drawing the screen, waits for that one thread to be free.

exps.title: One long job
exps.change: CPU job none → 200 ms of synchronous work every half second · setTimeout(…, 10) still armed every 100 ms
exps.question: What happens to a timer that is due 10 ms from now while the job runs?

exps.title: Who goes first
exps.change: One script: setTimeout(cb, 0), then Promise.resolve().then(cb), then console.log(…)
exps.question: In what order do the three run?

exps.title: A promise chain that never yields
exps.change: Promise chain on · 400 callbacks of 0.5 ms, each queuing the next
exps.question: Each callback is tiny. What happens to I/O callbacks and frames while the chain runs?

exps.title: Split the job
exps.change: 200 ms job → 40 chunks of 5 ms, each queued at the back of the conveyor
exps.question: What happens to the longest gap between frames, and to how long the job takes?

exps.title: Hand it to a worker
exps.change: 200 ms job → posted to a worker thread; the result comes back as a message
exps.question: What happens to the loop, and to how long the job takes?

blurb: Two requests read the same value, both write, and one quietly undoes the other. Nothing crashes, so it hides.
title: Race Condition Workbench
lede: A race condition happens when two requests read the same thing, both decide what to write, and one quietly undoes the other. Nothing crashes, so it hides until there is real traffic.

exps.title: Two clerks, no protection
exps.change: 2 clerks × 100 deposits each · read the card, work out the new balance at the desk (1 s), walk back and write it
exps.question: How many of the 200 deposits never reach the card?

exps.title: Take the key first
exps.change: 4 clerks · a clerk takes the key from the hook before reading and hangs it back after writing
exps.question: Nothing is lost now. What happens to deposits per minute compared with no protection?

exps.title: Check the version
exps.change: Compare-and-swap: the card carries a version number; a write only lands if the version is still the one the clerk read, otherwise the clerk reads again and redoes the sum
exps.question: Going from 2 clerks to 4, what happens?

exps.title: Check, then book
exps.change: 3 clerks fill 24 seats · each checks the board for a free seat, fills in the form at the desk, then pins the seat
exps.question: Every clerk checked the seat was free. How many seats end up booked twice?

exps.title: It passed locally
exps.change: The same unprotected code · 1 clerk (a unit test), 2 clerks at a quiet moment (a manual test), 4 clerks when the office is busy (production)
exps.question: What do the tests show?

blurb: Broadcast means every node learns every value; the topology decides how many messages that costs and how long it takes.
title: Broadcast Workbench
lede: Broadcast means every node learns every value. Which nodes talk to which (the topology) decides how many messages that costs and how long it takes.

exps.title: Pick a topology
exps.change: Grid → ring → hubs · 25 nodes, 100 values a second, 100 ms per message
exps.question: Challenge 3d asks for fewer than 30 messages per value, a median under 400 ms and a maximum under 600 ms. Which topology meets it?

exps.title: Batch the messages
exps.change: Hubs · batching off → one message per neighbour every 200 ms
exps.question: Challenge 3e asks for fewer than 20 messages per value, a median under 1 s and a maximum under 2 s. With batching every 200 ms…

exps.title: Cut the network
exps.change: Hubs · the fence goes up between columns 2 and 3 for 3 seconds · no retries
exps.question: What happens to the values sent while the network is cut?

exps.title: Lose a hub
exps.change: Hubs · the top-left hub is switched off
exps.question: Which nodes stop hearing new values?

exps.title: Forward everything
exps.change: Grid · forward every copy you receive, not only values you haven't seen
exps.question: One value enters the network. How many messages in the first second?

blurb: Every round, whoever knows tells a few random others. Nobody coordinates, nothing is retried, and everyone hears it fast.
title: Gossip Workbench
lede: Gossip spreads information the way a rumour moves through a village: every round, whoever knows tells a few random others. Nobody coordinates, nothing is retried, and yet everyone hears it fast.

exps.title: Ten times the village
exps.change: 40 houses → 400 houses · push, each house tells 2 random houses per round
exps.question: How many rounds until every house has heard the rumour?

exps.title: Tell more neighbours
exps.change: Fanout 1 → 3 · push, 40 houses
exps.question: Each house now tells 3 random houses per round instead of 1. What happens?

exps.title: Push, pull or both
exps.change: Push vs pull vs push-pull · fanout 1, 40 houses
exps.question: Once half the village knows, which way reaches the last houses fastest?

exps.title: Lose a third of the messages
exps.change: Message loss 0% → 30% · push-pull, fanout 2, 40 houses
exps.question: Three in ten messages vanish on the way. What happens to the rumour?

exps.title: How long before "dead"
exps.change: Failure timeout 4 → 8 → 16 rounds · heartbeats gossiped with fanout 2, slow links (3 in 10 messages arrive 1–3 rounds late)
exps.question: What does a short timeout do?

blurb: A log keeps records in arrival order and doesn't delete them on read; each consumer group keeps a bookmark instead.
title: Kafka Log Workbench
lede: A log keeps records in the order they arrive and doesn't delete them when they are read; each consumer group keeps a bookmark instead.

exps.title: Order per customer
exps.change: Records with no key (any track) vs keyed by customer · 3 tracks, 3 consumers, 4 records/s
exps.question: Each customer's records are created in order: created, paid, shipped. With no key, how often is a customer's record read before an earlier one of the same customer?

exps.title: A consumer crashes
exps.change: Consumer 1 crashes in the middle of a batch every 10 s · commit after processing vs before
exps.question: Committing after processing, what happens to the records it had processed but not yet committed when it crashed?

exps.title: More consumers than tracks
exps.change: 3 tracks · producer at 8 records/s · consumers in the group 3 → 6
exps.question: Three consumers can't keep up. With six, how many records are read per minute?

exps.title: A hot customer
exps.change: 70% of records are for customer A · keyed by customer · 3 tracks, 3 consumers, 4 records/s
exps.question: After a minute, where is the lag?

exps.title: Rebuild from the log
exps.change: After 90 s the customer totals are wiped · every bookmark is rewound to the oldest record and read again · keep all records vs keep 20 s
exps.question: Keeping every record, how many of the 6 customer totals come back right?

blurb: Counting sounds trivial until several machines count at once: lost updates, retries, and counters that never conflict.
title: Counter Workbench
lede: Counting sounds trivial until several machines count at once.

exps.title: Read, add one, write it back
exps.change: One shared key · each add reads the count, adds 1 and writes the result · 3 branches, 0.3 adds/s each, for 60 s
exps.question: Every add does its read and its write successfully. What share of the adds end up in the register?

exps.title: Compare-and-swap
exps.change: The write becomes "set to v + 1 only if it is still v" · on failure, read again and retry · traffic 0.1 → 0.6 adds/s per branch
exps.question: The count is now exact at both rates. What changes as traffic grows?

exps.title: One slot per branch
exps.change: Each branch writes only its own slot (its own count) · the total is the sum of all slots · 0.6 adds/s per branch, where compare-and-swap struggled
exps.question: How many adds are lost or retried now?

exps.title: Branch C is cut off
exps.change: One slot per branch · C's track is cut for 15 s, then healed · adds stop when it heals
exps.question: What happens to the count while C is cut off, and after?

exps.title: Reading right after an add
exps.change: Compare-and-swap · B adds 1 and gets its acknowledgement · at that moment A and B each read the count · 20 tries
exps.question: Does A's read include B's add?

title: Feature Flag Workbench
lede: A feature flag ships new code switched off and lets you decide, at run time, who sees it.
blurb: A feature flag ships new code switched off and lets you decide, at run time, who sees it.

exps.title: A bad feature at 50%
exps.change: Buggy feature on for 50% of users · someone notices at 30 s · flip the kill switch (servers refresh every 5 s) vs redeploy the old build (90 s pipeline, then 30 s per server)
exps.question: How long until no user hits the bug, with each fix?

exps.title: Random or sticky
exps.change: 30% rollout for 2 minutes · each request rolls a die vs each user is hashed to a fixed bucket
exps.question: Out of about 200 users, how many see both the old and the new version?

exps.title: Stale flags
exps.change: Feature on for everyone, turned off at 30 s · each server refreshes its copy of the settings every 5 s vs every 60 s
exps.question: With a 60 s refresh, how long do servers keep showing the feature after it's off?

exps.title: Flag debt
exps.change: 3 flags vs 10 flags in use, each on for half the users (sticky, independent)
exps.question: With 10 flags, how many different versions of the app are live at the same time?

exps.title: Staff first
exps.change: A buggy feature for 60 s · on for internal staff only (5% of traffic) vs on for 10% of all users
exps.question: How many customers hit the bug in that minute?

blurb: Readiness asks “can you take traffic now?”, liveness asks “do you need a restart?” Mix them up and blips become outages.
title: Health Probe Workbench
lede: Kubernetes asks every pod two different questions: can you take traffic right now (readiness), and are you so broken that only a restart will help (liveness)? Mixing them up turns small problems into outages.

exps.title: No readiness probe
exps.change: A deploy restarts shops 4 and 5 under steady traffic · readiness probe on → off
exps.question: Each restarted shop takes 12 s to open its doors and 10 s to stock its shelves. Without a readiness probe, what do customers see?

exps.title: Liveness checks the warehouse
exps.change: The warehouse (database) is down for 30 s · liveness checks the warehouse vs readiness checks it
exps.question: With the liveness probe checking the warehouse, when is the street fully open again?

exps.title: A tight timeout on a busy street
exps.change: Traffic at 90% of capacity · liveness timeout 5 s → 1 s
exps.question: The shops are slow but healthy: probes wait in the same queue as customers. What does a 1 s liveness timeout do?

exps.title: A slow start
exps.change: A shop takes 60 s to open its doors · liveness starts checking 10 s after start · no startup probe vs a startup probe
exps.question: Without a startup probe, when is the restarted shop ready?

exps.title: A jammed shop
exps.change: Shop 3 jams: its doors are open but nobody answers · readiness only vs readiness and liveness
exps.question: With only a readiness probe, what happens to shop 3?

blurb: Save to the database and tell other services in two writes, and a crash between them loses or invents events.
title: Outbox Workbench
lede: Most requests have to do two things: save something in the database and tell other services about it. Done as two separate writes, a failure in between leaves them disagreeing, and nothing reports it.

exps.title: Fail between the two writes
exps.change: Write the ledger, then post the letter · the clerk fails on the way to the postbox for 1 order in 20 · 10 minutes of orders
exps.question: Every ledger write succeeds before the clerk sets off. What does the warehouse end up with?

exps.title: Send first, then write
exps.change: Swap the order: post the letter, then write the ledger · the ledger write fails for 1 order in 20
exps.question: Does sending first fix it?

exps.title: Put the letter in the outbox
exps.change: The ledger card and the letter go into the cabinet in one transaction · a relay posts pending letters and then marks them sent · clerk fails 5%, relay fails 10% after posting, before marking
exps.question: What happens to lost and phantom orders now, and what new thing appears?

exps.title: The warehouse ships every letter
exps.change: Outbox, relay fails 10% after posting · warehouse dedupe off vs on (it keeps the order numbers it has seen and drops repeats)
exps.question: With dedupe off, what does the warehouse do with the repeated letters?

exps.title: A slower relay
exps.change: Outbox, nothing fails · the relay checks the outbox every 0.5 s, 2 s or 5 s · compared with walking the letter straight over
exps.question: What does a longer poll interval cost?

blurb: A lost reply makes the client pay again. An idempotency key lets the server spot the retry and replay the result.
title: Idempotency Workbench
lede: When a reply goes missing, the client can't tell whether its request worked, so it sends it again. An idempotency key lets the server recognise the retry and answer it with the result it already produced, instead of doing the work twice.

exps.title: Lost replies, no keys
exps.change: Keys off · 1 reply in 10 is lost on the way back · a customer who hears nothing in 5 s pays again · 4 customers, 3 minutes
exps.question: The counter charges correctly every time it receives a slip. Out of roughly 120 orders, how many end up charged twice?

exps.title: Remember the result
exps.change: Every order carries a key · the counter files key → receipt after charging · a slip whose key is on file gets the stored receipt back · same 10% loss
exps.question: What happens to the retries now?

exps.title: An impatient customer
exps.change: Customers wait only 1 s before paying again · charging takes 1.2–2.4 s · no replies lost · the key is filed only once the charge is done
exps.question: Keys are on and no reply is ever lost. How many orders are charged twice?

exps.title: Keys that expire
exps.change: Key lifetime 1 day → 8 s · 3 replies in 10 lost · retries back off 1, 2, 4 s, so a third try comes about 14 s after the first
exps.question: With the in-progress marker on, does a short key lifetime change anything?

exps.title: Same key, different amount
exps.change: A buggy client recalculates the total (+$5) on half of its retries but reuses the order's key · 3 replies in 10 lost · keys on
exps.question: What should the counter do with a retry whose key is on file but whose amount differs?

blurb: Flight, hotel, car, card: no shared transaction, so when a late step fails a saga undoes the earlier ones in reverse.
title: Saga Workbench
lede: Booking a trip touches several services that share no transaction: the flight, the hotel, the car, the card. A saga runs each step on its own and, when a later one fails, runs the undo of every earlier step.

exps.title: A card is declined after everything is booked
exps.change: No saga · each counter is called in turn and nothing is undone · 20% of cards are declined · 3 minutes of customers
exps.question: The flight, hotel and car are booked, then the card is declined. What happens to those three bookings?

exps.title: Undo calls that time out
exps.change: Saga · a quarter of undo calls time out, and half of those actually ran before the reply was lost · 40% of cards declined
exps.question: Compare three policies for a timed-out undo: give up, retry, or retry with the same idempotency key. What does each leave behind?

exps.title: Send the confirmation first
exps.change: Order: email → flight → hotel → car → payment, instead of email last · 20% of cards declined
exps.question: Of the trips that fail after the email went out, how many customers received a confirmation?

exps.title: Few seats, busy day
exps.change: 5 seats on each board · a customer every 2.5 s · 40% of cards declined · payment checked last
exps.question: Customers are turned away because the flight is full. How many of them were blocked by a seat held by a trip that was later undone?

exps.title: Drop the orchestrator
exps.change: Choreography: each counter hands the folder to the next directly, and back on failure · no desk, no checklist
exps.question: What changes?

blurb: One query for the list, then one per row. Each is a round trip, so it's invisible locally and slow in staging.
title: N+1 Query Workbench
lede: A list page runs one query for the list, then one more for each row's related data: N + 1 queries where 2 would do. Each is a round trip, so the page costs the number of rows times the distance to the database.

exps.title: The database moves away
exps.change: N+1 · 20 orders, 5 items each · database on the same host (0.2 ms round trip) → in another zone (10 ms)
exps.question: The page runs the same 21 queries and fetches the same 28 KB. How long does it take now?

exps.title: A bigger page
exps.change: Database in another zone · orders per page 20 → 50 · N+1 vs batched (one IN query for all the items)
exps.question: How does the page time change for each?

exps.title: One more level
exps.change: N+1 · 20 orders, 5 items each · the page now also shows each item's product, loaded the same lazy way
exps.question: How many queries does one page run now?

exps.title: JOIN or batch?
exps.change: Database in another zone · 50 orders with 50 items each · one JOIN (orders × items) vs two batched queries
exps.question: Which loads the page faster?

exps.title: Fire them all at once
exps.change: Database in another zone · 20 orders · the 20 item queries run 5 at a time on a connection pool, instead of one by one
exps.question: Compared with batching the items into one query…

blurb: When a hot cache entry expires, every request misses at once and the database takes the whole herd.
title: Cache Stampede Workbench
lede: A cache hides how much work the database would have to do. When a hot entry expires, every request that arrives before it is rebuilt misses at once and the database gets that hidden load in one burst.

exps.title: Everything expires at once
exps.change: A deploy fills 50 keys at the same moment, all with a 30 s TTL · 500 requests a second spread evenly · the oven has 8 shelves and bakes in 0.2 s, so it can take 40 orders a second
exps.question: What happens around the 30 s mark?

exps.title: Add ±20 % jitter
exps.change: Same deploy · every TTL is multiplied by a random factor between 0.8 and 1.2
exps.question: What happens to the busiest second at the oven?

exps.title: One order per tray
exps.change: One hot key at 500 requests a second · 10 s TTL · 0.2 s bake · a miss now waits for the order already in the oven instead of sending its own (single-flight, request coalescing)
exps.question: How many oven orders does each expiry cause now?

exps.title: Serve the old loaf
exps.change: Same hot key, but a bake now takes 1 s · single-flight vs stale-while-revalidate (serve the expired loaf at once and refresh it with one background order)
exps.question: With single-flight, about 500 customers wait up to a second at every expiry. With stale-while-revalidate…

exps.title: A slower oven
exps.change: One hot key at 200 requests a second · every miss orders · bake time 0.2 s → 1 s (five times slower)
exps.question: What happens to the longest wait at an expiry?

blurb: Connections are slow to open and the database holds few. Most pool trouble is sizing, leaks and holding one too long.
title: Connection Pool Workbench
lede: Opening a database connection is slow, and a database can only hold so many. A pool keeps a few open and lends them out; most connection trouble comes from sizing it, holding a connection too long or never giving it back.

exps.title: A new connection for every request
exps.change: No pool · each request opens its own connection, uses it once and closes it · 2 instances, 60 requests/s each
exps.question: The queries take about 10 ms. How long does a typical request take now?

exps.title: A bigger pool
exps.change: 2 instances at 500 requests/s each, more than the database can serve · pool per instance 5 → 10 → 20 (up to 10, 20 or 40 queries at once)
exps.question: Which pool size gets the most requests served per second?

exps.title: One code path forgets to give it back
exps.change: 1 request in 500 returns early without releasing its connection · 2 instances, pool 10, 60 requests/s each, for 5 minutes (Watch uses 1 in 50 at ×8, so the lots fill while you look)
exps.question: What do you see over those 5 minutes?

exps.title: An API call inside the transaction
exps.change: Each request calls an external API (200 ms) while holding its connection, instead of before taking one · 2 instances, pool 10, 60 requests/s each
exps.question: The database runs exactly the same queries. What happens?

exps.title: Scale out for a busy day
exps.change: Pool 20 per instance, the database allows 60 connections · scale from 2 to 4 instances · then the same through a pooler that keeps 20 server connections
exps.question: Connecting directly, what happens when the extra instances start?

blurb: Every metric label multiplies the series you store, and every trace costs space, so what you record must be chosen.
title: Cardinality Workbench
lede: Every label on a metric multiplies how many time series it creates, and every trace you keep costs storage, so what you record has to be chosen.

exps.title: Add a status label
exps.change: http_requests_total{method, route} → {method, route, status} · 2 methods × 8 routes, status has 5 values · 100 requests/s for an hour
exps.question: The metric had 16 series. After adding status, how many series does it have?

exps.title: Add user_id
exps.change: {method, route, status} → {method, route, status, user_id} · 10,000 active users · 100 requests/s for an hour
exps.question: Compared with the 80 series before, the count after one hour is…

exps.title: Raw paths as the route
exps.change: route="/orders/{id}" → route="/orders/58213" · ids come from a catalogue of a million · {method, route, status} · 100 requests/s
exps.question: How many series after one hour, and after a day?

exps.title: Head sampling at 1%
exps.change: Keep 1 in 100 traces, decided when the request starts · 0.1% of requests fail · one rare bug hits 1 in 10,000 · 100 requests/s, 12 hours
exps.question: Each hour about 360 requests fail, 36 of them from the rare bug. How many traces of the rare bug do you keep in an hour?

exps.title: Tail sampling
exps.change: Wait until each trace finishes, then keep every error, every slow trace (0.5%) and 1% of the rest · same traffic as before
exps.question: Compared with head sampling at 1%, what does tail sampling cost?

blurb: Wait until events stop, then act once. Every keystroke restarts the wait, so a burst becomes one request.
title: Debounce Workbench
lede: A debounce waits until events stop for a moment and then acts once. Every new event restarts the wait, so a burst of keystrokes becomes one request.

exps.title: Debounce the search box
exps.change: Search-as-you-type · every keystroke used to send a request · now: wait until 300 ms with no key, then send once
exps.question: Someone types a search of about 12 characters, pausing briefly between words. How many requests does one search send now?

exps.title: Choose the wait
exps.change: Same typing · the debounce wait 100 ms → 300 ms → 1 s · a steady server that answers in about 0.2 s
exps.question: What does each wait give you?

exps.title: A key held down
exps.change: An event every 50 ms for 5 s (a held key, a scroll, a window resize), then 2 s of quiet · debounce 300 ms
exps.question: When does the first request go out?

exps.title: A double click on Submit
exps.change: An impatient user double-clicks the order button, the clicks about 160 ms apart · no debounce, trailing 300 ms, or leading 300 ms
exps.question: Which setting sends exactly one order, and sends it immediately?

exps.title: Slow answers arrive late
exps.change: Typing with a server that is usually quick but takes 1 to 2.5 s for one request in six · no debounce, debounce 300 ms, then debounce plus cancelling the older request
exps.question: With a 300 ms debounce, can the screen still show results for an older search after a newer one?

blurb: Run the handler at most once per interval while events keep coming: steady updates during a scroll, the rest dropped.
title: Throttle Workbench
lede: Some events arrive far faster than you need to act on them: a scroll or a pointer fires 60 to 120 times a second. A throttle lets the handler run at most once per interval, keeps the newest event and drops the rest.

exps.title: Throttle a scroll handler
exps.change: A scroll fires 120 events a second · the handler takes 6 ms · no gate → throttle, 100 ms
exps.question: While the user is scrolling, how often does the handler run with the throttle?

exps.title: Leading edge only
exps.change: Throttle 100 ms · run on the leading edge only (no trailing call) · scroll in bursts, then stop
exps.question: When the user stops scrolling, does the handler see the position they stopped at?

exps.title: Throttle or debounce a drag
exps.change: A steady 3 s drag at 60 events a second · throttle 100 ms → debounce 100 ms
exps.question: How many updates does each give during the drag itself?

exps.title: Throttle the add-to-cart button
exps.change: Bursts of quick clicks, one every 130–220 ms · each click should add one item · throttle 500 ms
exps.question: What happens to the cart?

exps.title: Pick the interval
exps.change: Scrolling at 120 events a second · throttle interval 16 ms (one frame) → 100 ms → 500 ms
exps.question: What does a longer interval buy, and what does it cost?

blurb: First in, first out. Between producers and workers a queue soaks up bursts and survives crashes, if you ack right.
title: Queue Workbench
lede: A queue is a line: the first one in is the first one out. Put one between the code that creates work and the code that does it, and it soaks up bursts, survives crashed workers and keeps arrival order, as long as the work keeps up on average.

exps.title: Slightly more than the clerks can do
exps.change: Arrivals 8/s → 10/s · three clerks can do 9 a second between them · run for 5 minutes
exps.question: After 5 minutes at 10 a second, what does the queue look like?

exps.title: 200 parcels at once
exps.change: A quiet 5/s stream that the clerks (9/s) easily keep up with · 200 parcels dropped in at once · a queue vs nowhere to wait (turned away if every clerk is busy)
exps.question: What happens to the 200 parcels?

exps.title: A clerk collapses before stamping
exps.change: 1 try in 10 ends with the clerk collapsing: half during the work, half after it but before the stamp · stamp after the work vs stamp on pickup vs an idempotent handler
exps.question: With the stamp after the work, what happens to the parcels whose clerk collapsed?

exps.title: One parcel in 50 can never be processed
exps.change: 4 clerks, 1.5 s per parcel, 2 arriving a second · a bad parcel fails every time · retried forever vs moved to the dead-letter cage after 3 tries · 5 minutes
exps.question: With retry forever, what happens by the 5-minute mark?

exps.title: One slow parcel at the front
exps.change: Parcels must be handled in order · one parcel for customer A takes 30 s instead of 0.4 s · one order for everything vs one order per customer (4 customers)
exps.question: How long do customers B, C and D wait?

blurb: Last in, first out: every function call, every undo, and under overload, which users still get an answer in time.
title: Stack Workbench
lede: A stack hands back the last thing you put on it: last in, first out. It runs every function call you make, it is how undo works, and under overload it can decide which users get an answer.

exps.title: A function that calls itself
exps.change: sum(5) = 5 + sum(4), …, down to sum(1) = 1 · every call waits for the one it made
exps.question: How deep does the call stack get, and which call returns first?

exps.title: Recursion that goes too deep
exps.change: The same sum, n = 5,000 · the stack has room for 1,000 frames · then the same sum written as a loop
exps.question: What happens to the recursive version?

exps.title: Undo twice, then type
exps.change: Type A, B, C · undo twice (C and B move to the redo stack) · then type D
exps.question: What can Redo bring back now?

exps.title: Walking a tree with a stack
exps.change: Tree: 1 has children 2 and 3; 2 has 4 and 5; 3 has 6 and 7 · keep the nodes still to visit on a stack (or let recursion do it)
exps.question: Which node is visited right after node 2?

exps.title: Overloaded: newest first or oldest first?
exps.change: Requests arrive at 120% of what the worker can finish · clients give up after 1 s · 60 s, six seeded runs
exps.question: What share of requests finish before their client gives up?
